idiom_name: translation-unit module of free functions (opaque handles, function-pointer table when implementations vary)
implementation_notes: C has no classes, so the service is a translation unit: a header declaring the domain operation's prototypes in model terms and a .c file whose helpers are static (file-private), with dependencies arriving as pointers to other modules' opaque handles or as plain data. Because there is no virtual dispatch, an interface with interchangeable implementations is modelled as a struct of function pointers - a hand-built vtable - passed in by the caller and kept immutable (static const); without that need, plain prefixed functions are simpler and faster. Error handling uses return codes with out-parameters instead of exceptions, and ownership must be documented: a domain function taking const pointers borrows, it never frees.
pitfalls: Without a class there is nothing stopping a 'stateless' service from caching the last result or the current session in a file-scope static variable - that is hidden global state and a data race; pass everything as parameters.

Ownership is manual: whoever allocates an Invoice* must free it, and the service must not take ownership of the const pointers it borrows. Nothing in the compiler enforces that contract, so document it in the header.
Const-correctness is the only protection against a service mutating its operands: without const on every borrowed pointer, the callee can quietly change the very state it is supposed to leave alone.
